::: {.lead}
The online races of *Pocket Quest* need servers: for the races, for the
leaderboard, for the saved progress of every player. Byte Bay could buy
servers and put them in a cupboard of the office. But on launch day ten
times more players come than on a normal day, and at night almost nobody
plays. In lectures 19 and 20 you saw how devices reach a server over the
Internet. In this lesson you learn where such servers live today: in the
**cloud**. You learn the service models, the kinds of cloud, how the cloud
grows with the players, and what can go wrong. Every section ends with a
short task.
:::

## Key terms

{{< glossary cloud-computing data-centre cloud-region virtual-machine iaas paas saas baas public-cloud private-cloud hybrid-cloud scalability pay-as-you-go vendor-lock-in >}}

## 21.1 What is the cloud?

The cloud is not in the sky: it is other people's computers, in big
buildings, rented over the Internet (@fig-own).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 21.1 — Cloud computing"}
**Cloud computing** means using computing power, storage and software from
a provider over the Internet, **when you need it**, and paying for what you
use (**pay-as-you-go**). The provider runs **data centres** with thousands
of servers in **regions** around the world. One real server runs many
**virtual machines**.
:::

![Own servers or the cloud.](images/own-or-cloud.png){#fig-own width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.1 — Two ways to run the races"}
1. **Own servers:** Byte Bay buys 10 servers for the launch peak. They cost
   money every day, also at night, and a broken disk is Byte Bay's problem.
2. **Cloud:** Byte Bay rents race servers by the hour, in a region near its
   players, and gives them back when the players leave.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"The cloud is free and always online." Cloud services cost money per use,
and providers also have outages. Plan for both.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Cloud in your day"}
List three cloud services you used today (for example e-mail, an online
office app, a game with cloud saves, a video service).

*Your result:* a list of three.
:::

## 21.2 Service models: IaaS, PaaS, SaaS and BaaS

The models differ in **who manages what** (@fig-models).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 21.2 — The service models"}
- **IaaS** (Infrastructure as a Service): you rent virtual machines,
  storage and networks; you manage the operating system and the software.
- **PaaS** (Platform as a Service): you upload your code and data; the
  provider runs the operating system and the runtime.
- **SaaS** (Software as a Service): you use a finished application, for
  example an online office suite.
- **BaaS** (Backend as a Service): ready services for apps and games, such
  as player accounts, cloud saves and leaderboards, used through an SDK.
:::

![Who manages what in each model.](images/service-models.png){#fig-models width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.2 — Four ways to run the leaderboard"}
1. **IaaS:** a rented virtual machine; Rami installs the OS updates, the
   database and the code.
2. **PaaS:** Rami uploads only the leaderboard code; the platform runs it.
3. **BaaS:** the game uses the leaderboard service of a game back end; no
   server code at all.
4. More control means more work: IaaS gives the most control, BaaS the
   least work.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/cloud-stack.html" poster="sims/cloud-stack.png" title="Cloud Stack: who manages what?" height="680" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Thinking that with SaaS or BaaS the studio has no responsibility. It still
decides which player data it stores, who can see it, and how long it keeps
it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Who manages it?"}
1. In **Cloud Stack**, set the layers right for IaaS, PaaS and SaaS.
2. For each, write one thing that Byte Bay still manages.

*Your result:* three correct stacks and three sentences.
:::

## 21.3 Public, private and hybrid cloud

Besides the model, a cloud differs in **who shares it** (@fig-deploy).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 21.3 — Kinds of cloud"}
- **Public cloud:** a provider sells services to many customers over the
  Internet.
- **Private cloud:** cloud technology for one organization only, in its own
  or a rented data centre.
- **Hybrid cloud:** own servers or a private cloud work together with a
  public cloud.
:::

![Public, private and hybrid cloud.](images/deployment.png){#fig-deploy width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.3 — Three choices"}
1. Byte Bay uses a **public cloud** for the races: cheap and fast to start.
2. A partner bank keeps payment data in a **private cloud**.
3. Byte Bay keeps its build PCs in the office and adds public cloud servers
   for launch peaks: a **hybrid cloud**.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
"Private cloud means more secure, always." Security depends on the people
and the settings; a small private cloud with weak settings is less safe
than a well-run public cloud.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Choose the kind"}
Which kind fits? (a) a student team with no money for servers; (b) a
ministry that must keep data inside the country, on its own servers; (c) a
studio with office servers that needs extra power once a month.

*Your result:* three answers.
:::

## 21.4 Scaling, cost and risks

The biggest strength of the cloud is that it can grow and shrink with the
players (@fig-scale). It also has risks (@fig-pros).

::: {.callout-important title="Definition 21.4 — Scalability, and the risks"}
**Scalability** is the ability to add or remove servers as the number of
users changes; **auto-scaling** does it by itself, by rules such as "add a
server when 80 % are busy". With pay-as-you-go, quiet hours cost less. The
risks: costs that grow with use, **outages** of the provider, **vendor
lock-in** (special services make moving hard), and data laws about where
player data may be stored.
:::

![Launch day with fixed servers and with auto-scaling.](images/scaling.png){#fig-scale width=94%}

![Benefits and risks.](images/cloud-pros-cons.png){#fig-pros width=94%}

::: {.callout-note title="Example 21.4 — Launch day"}
1. With 5 fixed servers, about 3,700 players cannot join at 19:00.
2. With 9 fixed servers, nobody is turned away, but most servers do nothing
   from midnight to noon.
3. With auto-scaling, the servers follow the players: nobody is turned away,
   and the day costs less than with 9 fixed servers.
:::

{{< sim file="sims/scale-sim.html" poster="sims/scale-sim.png" title="Launch Day Scaling: enough servers, not too many" height="680" >}}

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistake"}
Auto-scaling with no upper limit and no budget alert. A bug or an attack
can start hundreds of servers. Set a maximum and a cost alarm.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Do it · Play the day"}
In **Launch Day Scaling**, find the smallest number of fixed servers that
turns nobody away, and compare its cost with auto-scaling.

*Your result:* two costs and one sentence.
:::

## Case study: Cloud Match

Byte Bay and its partners have six jobs: a race server that needs a special
OS setting; a small leaderboard program; shared documents for the team;
accounts, cloud saves and a leaderboard through an SDK; payment data of a
bank that must stay in its own data centre; and build PCs in the office with
extra cloud servers for launch peaks. The Game challenge of the interactive
lesson uses these jobs. In the mini-game below you match each job with the
right model or kind of cloud.

{{< sim file="sims/cloud-match.html" poster="sims/cloud-match.png" title="Cloud Match: the right cloud for each job" kind="game" height="460" >}}

## Further reading

Mell and Grance, *The NIST Definition of Cloud Computing*, NIST Special
Publication 800-145 (2011). Erl, Mahmood and Puttini, *Cloud Computing:
Concepts, Technology & Architecture* (2013), Chapters 3–4.

## Exercises

1. Explain cloud computing in one sentence.
2. What is a data centre?
3. What is a virtual machine?
4. In IaaS, who installs the operating system updates?
5. In PaaS, what does the studio upload?
6. Give one example of SaaS.
7. What does BaaS offer a game?
8. What is the difference between a public and a private cloud?
9. What is auto-scaling?
10. Name two risks of the cloud.

## Answers to the exercises

::: {.answers}
1. Using computing power, storage and software from a provider over the
   Internet, when needed, and paying for the use.
2. A building with many servers, power, cooling and network links.
3. A computer made in software on a real server.
4. The customer (the studio).
5. Its code and data.
6. For example an online office suite or web e-mail.
7. Ready services such as accounts, cloud saves and leaderboards.
8. A public cloud serves many customers; a private cloud serves one
   organization.
9. Adding and removing servers by itself when the load changes.
10. For example costs, outages, vendor lock-in, data laws.
:::
